property_summary: After any call to fallback with admissible input, the contract's balance must either be zero (if transferred) or at least 10 ether; the buggy version requires 0 ether which can cause subsequent transfers with non-zero value to fail the first require, but the property specifically captures that a successful call with msg.value=0 can lead to a balance contradiction with the reference's requirement of 10 ether minimum deposit.

After any successful fallback call, if the ether was not transferred to the sender (i.e., when block.number % 15 != 0), the contract's balance must be at least the value sent in that call; the buggy contract breaks this by allowing a zero-ether call to succeed and set pastBlockTime without enforcing a minimum balance increase.

After any successful fallback call that does not transfer the balance (block.number % 15 != 0), the contract's balance must equal the sum of all msg.value sent in successful calls since deployment; the buggy version breaks this by allowing msg.value == 0 to succeed, causing the balance to fall below this invariant.

After any successful fallback call that does not transfer the balance (when block.number % 15 != 0), the contract's balance must be strictly greater than it was before the call; the buggy version violates this by allowing a zero-value call to succeed without increasing the balance.

Correct C requires msg.value == 10 ether on every fallback call; the mutant allows any msg.value, causing the balance-check transfer condition to execute for non-10-ether deposits, which breaks the invariant that ether can only be transferred when exactly 10 ether was sent.
In the correct contract, ether can be transferred out only when the fallback is called with exactly 10 ether, whereas the mutant allows transfers for any msg.value, potentially draining funds.

The reference contract always updates pastBlockTime to block.timestamp and enforces that block.timestamp > pastBlockTime before the update, while the mutant skips this check, allowing pastBlockTime to be updated with the same or a past timestamp when called repeatedly in the same block or after a warp backwards.

After multiple valid fallback calls that do not trigger a transfer, the pastBlockTime must advance; the buggy version leaves it stuck at zero, causing the timestamp check to fail on all subsequent calls except possibly the very first.

After any successful call that does NOT trigger the balance transfer (i.e. block.number % 15 != 0), a subsequent successful call with a strictly later block.timestamp must revert in the buggy version because pastBlockTime is never updated, while the correct version updates it and thus succeeds.
After any successful fallback call, the pastBlockTime must equal the block.timestamp of that call; the buggy version leaves pastBlockTime at its previous value, violating this invariant.

For any two consecutive successful fallback calls with the second at a strictly later block.timestamp, the value of pastBlockTime after the second call must equal the block.timestamp of the second call; the buggy version fails to update pastBlockTime, so it retains the timestamp of the first call.

The reference C transfers its entire balance to the caller when block.number is divisible by 15, while the buggy version retains the balance; after any valid fallback call, the contract's balance must be zero if the block number is divisible by 15 and non-zero otherwise.

After any valid call to fallback, the contract's balance must be less than or equal to the balance before the call; the reference contract respects this invariant by potentially transferring its balance away, while the buggy contract never transfers, causing its balance to increase with every call and eventually violate the invariant.

After any valid fallback call, pastBlockTime equals the block.timestamp of that call; the reference always sets it, the buggy version also sets it, so the difference is that in the reference the contract's ether balance after the call is zero if block.number % 15 == 0, while the buggy version never transfers ether and its balance grows, thus after any two valid calls where the second's block.number % 15 == 0, the reference balance is 0 and the buggy balance is positive — but simpler: after a valid call where block.number % 15 == 0, the reference balance is 0 and the buggy balance is >0.
After a valid fallback call, if the block number is a multiple of 15, the contract's balance must be zero; the reference transfers the balance, while the buggy version retains it.

After any number of valid fallback calls the contract's ETH balance never exceeds its cumulative received value minus transfers triggered when block.number % 15 == 0; the reference satisfies this, but the buggy version never transfers and its balance grows exactly by every 10 ETH received, eventually violating the invariant.

For any admissible call, the contract's ETH balance after the fallback should be zero when and only when block.number is divisible by 15; the buggy version transfers the balance when block.number is NOT divisible by 15, leaving the balance zero for divisible chains and non-zero otherwise.

After any admissible call to fallback with exactly 10 ether, the contract's balance becomes 0 if and only if block.number % 15 == 0; the buggy version instead sets balance to 0 when block.number % 15 != 0, violating the rule.

After any fallback call, pastBlockTime must equal block.timestamp; the buggy mutation sets pastBlockTime before the time check, making the require fail when timestamps are equal, thus leaving pastBlockTime unchanged from a previous call, which violates equality.
